newsitem.title: Nigeria: Nigerian motor show opens amidst economic gloom.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian motor show opens amidst economic gloom.

text.p: Matthew Tostevin
A Nigerian motor-show opened on Friday amidst gloom over the state of vehicle sales in the depressed economy.
"There are not as many exhibitors as there were a few years ago, the economy is so wobbly," Yewande Ayo, organiser of Automania, told Reuters.
At one time Africa's most populous nation had six vehicle assembly plants. Now it has only one -- run by Peugeot Automobiles Nigeria.

"Business is very dull. Very, very dull. We're here at the show in one more effort to try and improve things," said Sola Ajidagba of CFAO Motors, distributors for Mitsubishi, Land Rover, Daewoo and Iveco.
"All sectors have been hit although commercial vehicles are marginally better than the rest, we are having to look at new strategies to increase sales."
Ajidagba said CFAO had cut profit margins and introduced hire-purchase terms over 24 months, as well as increasing spending on publicity.
"In the past we waited for customers to come to the sales rooms, now we have to get out to them," he said.
Since Volkswagen and Fiat closed their assembly plants Peugeot is the only company to produce as much as 35 percent of the components of its vehicles inside Nigeria itself.
Production at the plant in the northern city of Kaduna has risen to around 30 vehicles per day in 1996 from 15 to 20 in 1995.
But this is far below the 150 per day in 1991 and 260 per day in the early 1980s, when Nigeria still rode high on the oil boom.
The economic decline was accelerated by a wave of strikes and riots which followed the annulment of presidential elections in 1993 by a previous military government.
A four-fold fuel price hike in 1994, shortage of foreign exchange and lack of confidence in the economy saw inflation running above 80 percent a year.
While relative macroeconomic stability has returned, there is still no sign of increased demand.

"Before business in Nigeria was fantastic, now the market is shrinking, so competition is increasing, prices are coming down and so are margins," said Frederic Larrouilh of French group SOEXIMEX, which imports spare parts.
Nigeria is a centre for the whole of West and Central Africa as a source of motor spares, but surrounding economies are performing little better than Nigeria's own, and in many cases worse.
"We are forced to diversify and are looking at other import businesses, Nigeria is a huge potential market," Larrouilh said.
Facing difficulties in sourcing foreign exchange he said SOEXIMEX had begun exporting cocoa to pay for imports.
Notably absent from the show were Nigeria's biggest car importers -- those bringing second hand cars, often in doubtful working order, from Europe.
Official statistics show over 85,000 used cars were imported in 1995, compared to 15,000 new cars. Unofficially, used car imports are likely to be higher.
"From those that I know I can tell you the used car importers are also suffering," said Ajidagba.
